title: A Dynamically Reconfigurable Digital-Integrated Voltage-Regulator Fabric for Energy-Efficient DVFS in Multi-Domain soCs
problem: Conventional SoC voltage-regulator (VR) architectures use static domain grouping and fixed buck topologies determined at design time. However, SoC domains continuously undergo power-state transitions with changing voltage and current loads; static groupings cannot dynamically reconfigure to maximize efficiency, precluding runtime voltage scaling optimizations.
motivation: Energy efficiency is critical for modern SoCs; dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) is a primary power-management technique, but static VR architectures leave efficiency gains on the table.
method: The system uses a reconfigurable voltage-regulator fabric—a power-delivery circuit that can reprogram its connections while the chip is running—to adapt to changing power demands. As processor domains shift between active and idle states, the fabric dynamically reassigns which regulators service which domains, and when peak current isn't needed, it simplifies multi-stage buck converters (voltage step-down circuits) down to fewer stages. It also switches simpler voltage regulators called LDOs (which waste less power when the voltage difference is small) into the configuration to reduce losses further. This continuous adaptation to real-time conditions makes the overall power delivery more efficient than fixed designs.
key_novelty: The core innovation is a voltage-regulator system that dynamically reconfigures itself while running—reorganizing which processor domains it powers and adapting which regulator types it uses—to improve efficiency across changing power demands.
contributions: Dynamically reconfigurable voltage-regulator fabric for multi-domain SoCs
Runtime domain regrouping reflecting power-state transitions
Multi-phase buck disaggregation for improved current efficiency
LDO assignment optimization to minimize dropout losses
